blocks.x: Okay, I guess it's going if you want to give your name. You don't have to get close, just sit back and relax.
Okay.
You don't pick up anything in the room.
So my name is Al Morgan.
Is there any middle name by the way?
No, my full name called me Albert. But I don't know. I've always interviewed everybody I went to, he says, they're like Al for short.
I don't remember until last night I heard somebody call you Albert. When were you born? Do you remember your birth date exactly?
Oh, yes. I was born about 42 years ago. It's August 19th, by the way, today is my birthday. Oh, exactly.
What a diamond. What was the year then? It seems 19.
Oh, boy. Let me see. We'll have to go.
42 years.
Like that. That should be, for now, about 1912. 1912. Something like that.
Yeah. Well, anyway. It's about. Well, it's close. Yeah. Can you remember your first music you ever heard when you were a kid? Was it your brothers playing?

Well, yes. I remember a lot about my brothers playing way before I ever started, see, because... You're a disembarker. You're a disembarker. Yeah. It's a long distance microphone. Yeah. And my brother, Sam especially, he was the oldest one, and he's always played the trumpet, see. And I, from a young kid, I used to like to hear him play. And the band he had then, during those years, when I was a kid, and I was crazy about bass playing, you see.
Yeah, he was one of the greatest of the best players.
So, perhaps you heard of the Simon Morera?
Oh, yes. I know Lawrence.
Yeah. Yes, yes, the brother.
And, um...
We had another brother. John Morera. John John. That's right. He used to play with the Tuxedo Band, wasn't it?
Went to New York and died in the 1940s.
Oh, is that so?
Nine years ago.
Let's see. I'm sorry.
But Lawrence is living there.
That's the same... In the 40s. 40s. Same year I was in New York. Ron Ryan. Yeah, you should have been.
Jimmy Ryan. I never met him, but I remember when I was there in 19... I was there exactly in 1940, and they said, John Morera lives up the Red Alive where he was. Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
It seems like just, oh, two or three years later, he was dead. Pretty sure, but in 1943 he died. Because that's when I met Lawrence in 1942. I would be glad to go.
Well, I do remember the first... This is why I say mention Simon, because he was the first man that I had in mind playing bass.
Do you remember their father, Billy?
No, I don't remember the father, but I heard a lot of him.
You're in his theory around him.
Yes. How many say he was a great bass player in those days?
What part of town is your... Where were you born in? What part of town were you raised?
Well, I was raised around... around Ursuline and Dauphin, around that territory. That's more of the French part of town.
French...
Italian, you know. Near the French market, up there. Because Sam used to live there. Ursuline and Dauphin. Near Bourbon.
Sam's wife still lives on Ursuline, I believe, back...
A little further back. Back...
But they still live in that same...
Yeah.
Back near the...
Yeah.
In the Ray, along in there.
They've always lived around in the French market part of town.
And you remember the earliest bands you heard with your brothers? Did your mother and father play anything with them?
No. No, no.
Did the musical sing any of them?
No. All my people was... Baptist, you know, religion type of people. I think it's... Everything, when they start this music business, it started with Sam. And then on, the brothers picked it up.
Sam was the oldest one.

Yes, he was. He was the oldest one. And then Robert, the one that died not very long ago. Last... No, I know you don't know him. Well, he never did play music, you see. And then Isaiah, Andrew, and myself.
Can you remember any of the early bands you heard aside from your brother's band?
Well, yes. You mean the recordings?
No, no. It was real early when you were a kid. Oh. And you were too young to go to a dance scene.
Yes. Oh, yes.
I have... Parades are what you heard of when you were...

Yeah, oh, yes. I used to watch parades. It's one of the most fabulous things, you know. It's fascinating, you know. See, I've enjoyed parades. Sometimes the boys used to get pretty rough and follow those second liners, you know. People had... People had... Youngsters had bad ideas. And during those days, there were different gangs and meet through parades and start fights and so on like that. I guess the music was driving them wild during those days.
One ward to another and the other gang wouldn't want them to come into their territory or something.
Yes.
Nothing like that goes on now, but the parades are still pretty good.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I remember all the funerals and so on like that and how they would play going and coming back.
You still have all that?

I've heard many people ask about those stories of New Orleans and all the bands and what they do. It's true. And so I says, for sure. I had a Jimmy Ryan's on 52nd Street. We used to meet lots of kids, college kids. And they would ask me about different things like that. I says, well, it's true. As much as I could think back, you know, think of.
When you started in music, what was your first instrument?

Yes, my first instrument was bass because it was fascinating to me. I used to watch, sit there and watch Simon and Maria. And my brother, my oldest brother, used to watch this. Don't bother that man. Let him play his instrument. I'll never forget an assignment to my brother. One day, he says, Sam, you don't know. I said, this boy might be a great bass player someday.
Let him go if you want to learn.
Another fellow used to play trombone. His name was, I think, Hank. Hank.
All I knew was Jim Robinson later on in the last year.
No, no, no. Before Jim Robinson. Hank is... Yank? Yank or Hank?
Oh, you're Yank Johnson.
Yes, from... From... From... From... Al J.
Yeah, two brothers. Buddy Johnson and...
Yes, Buddy Johnson. That's right. Yes, that's right.
He died a long time ago. Nobody I've ever talked to knew anything about him. You're about the first one that's mentioned him since Bunk Johnson.
Is that so? Yes. Oh, wonderful trombone player.
So, Yank was in that band.
Yes, yes. He was... Him and his drummer then was Alfred. Alfred... Oh, geez. I forgot the last name. That guy. He was a fine drummer.
Could be Alfred Williams.
Could be.
He came out with Ori and Professor Renter.
Yes, yes, yes. Yeah. That's sticking.
He still plays the parades with the Eureka Band.

Oh, I think so. Yes. He's going that over with the drum. Oh, he was a wonderful drummer, that guy. Oh, my brother had some fine men with him. And during that time, let me see, who played guitar? I'm trying to think who played... It wasn't guitar then. It was banjo. Yeah. It was Johnny. Johnny Dave. Johnny Dave.
I don't know. Was there a fellow by the name of Kimball played? There was an old man, Kimball.
Oh, yeah. I know old man, Kimball, and his son. But he wasn't playing with my brother then. It was... It was a...
It was a fellow by the name of...
Dave. Johnny Dave. I don't know.
It's something like that. Older Brothers or Lower Energy.
Yeah. And let me see now. And before... Now, the bass player was working with him during those big days of my brother. Do you know Sidney Brown? They call him Jim Little.
He's...

Jim Little. Yeah. Well, Jim Little was in Isaiah's band. See? That's right. There were two bands. Yeah. See? It was two Morgan bands. That's what I'm trying to break down now. And I... I don't have all that space.
I'm not sure Isaiah can straighten us out. Yeah. He'll give us a good account of that.
I'm trying to think of the bass player Sam had. He was a little guy and he had a great big bass. The first time I ever saw a console bass. It's a great big thing.
But the best artist...

No, let me see. I know his name if I heard him. He was a very fine bass player. He was the first guy outside of Simon Maria that... And old man Kimball that I've ever saw finger bass correctly. You see?
Jimmy Brown. Do you remember him?
Let me see. Jimmy Brown. Jimmy Brown.
Manuel Perez sometimes.
Manuel Perez. Jimmy Brown. I don't know. There's names now. It's really gone from me. I used to know that name.
Are there any other bass players you remember? Do you remember Jimmy Johnson when you were here?

Jimmy Johnson, yes. Mr. Johnson. I always called him Mr. Johnson. As a bass player. Yes, he was another one. He played up now mostly. Yeah. He was a fine bass player too. Yes, he did. All those men used to read very good. They were good readers. Like old man Kimball and Jimmy. And this fellow, I'm telling you, was my brother then. And then Simon, later on when I got with Simon, he was the first one who started me to read him. Showed me how to bow bass. And I'll never forget. And he was always right. He says, Al, that's what I'm showing you. Always remember to learn the bow. That's what these things are for.
Like you do last time. He says, bow.

Yes. He says, always learn the bow of the bass. And I started with him. And I used to practically live at his house. And I learned a lot from him. He used to repair his own bass and take them down. And I learned everything about a bass, fooling with him. When I was in the teaching.
How old were you when you first started this?
Oh, I was in my teens.
You could reach him all right.
Yeah, yeah. Oh, yes. I could reach.
Did you hear some of these? Oh, Johnny Lindsay was another bass player around.

Yes, yeah. Yeah, Johnny Lindsay. But I don't remember Johnny Lindsay as a bass player. He played trombone. Trombone, that's right. Now, I remember him. But I've heard, yeah. I've heard he was a bass player. Or with P. Ron. Oh, let me see. No, I don't remember Johnny Lindsay playing bass with P. Ron.
He played trombone with him, I think.

Well, maybe so. Yes, yes, he did. Because the bass player with P. Ron, I remember, was Eskader. Oh, yeah. Eskader. Yeah. He's a Spanish Cuban. He's a Cuban guy. Yes. Because he played bass, string bass and bass horn. And by the way, when I was with David John, and he had his band on the Astoria roof, he's the first lesson on the bass horn. He started me playing bass tuba.
I heard one rumor once that when you made those records, you were so young, you had to practically stand on a box.

No. No. No. No. No. But I was very young, though. He started me on both bass. Because I couldn't read very well. As a matter of fact, I just know a couple of notes. I've always knew my instruments. Because that's the first thing they started me from, the old foundation.
And when you started, did you have a three string bass or four?

No. No. But I could play three strings. I started with four. Simon Morrill was one. That's the first thing he told me, he said, you've got to play the right type of bass. You've got to learn to play the E strings. They're all played. He just wanted to think, it's note on all strings. So I started because, I'll tell you why, he had a bass method. That's why, you hear this man say, I used to pack my book around all the time. I had to pack the book to watch the notes. I was very serious about this, and the positions, and the different T's, and everything. I was studying hard, the hard way, you know, because I didn't have very much teaching right then and there, you know. So, but then I started playing around like the rest of the guys.
Oh, so do I get in? I'll turn it off for a second. Can you mind me a little bit more about that job at the Astoria Hotel, or what do they call it, the ballroom, really?

Yes, it was the Astoria Roof. Roof. Oh, it was on the roof, though. Yeah, well no, that's what they call it, Astoria Roof, yeah. David Jones developed a very fine band up there. It's one of the trombone players of Celestan's A, Tuxedo, probably the trombone, Bay, Bay, yeah. Yeah, that's the guy. And we had a nice little band for a long time up there. And then, and I stayed with him, and almost was about to learn to play that bass horn pretty fair. Yeah. Well, the big thing that happened to me, and started me on my real music career, right out of that Astoria Roof, Fait Myable stepped in then. He saw me, he saw me, so I never forget, so one night he come down and said, sit.

The kid said, I heard a lot of talk of you. I had to come down and look you over. I can see now what the people on there. He said, I'd like to take you on the boat with me. I told him, I said, well, I don't read. He said, well, that's all right. Many of them from here, everyone I've taken from here I couldn't read. But you will if you stick with me a long time. I said, well, I don't know. I'll try. So he'd come back again in the afternoon. So I made up my mind to go with him. About what year was that? Oh, that was in the early, the late 20th. The late 20th.
Before we go into that boat and all, you remember the very first job you ever played and the first band you ever played?

Yeah. Yeah. Well, it was during the time I was learning. When I first started, I bought the bass about the day after Lent, right after Mardi Gras. Yeah. The Simon Mare. He sold me a bass for $7. I'll never forget. And I had been working as a shoeshine boy then out on Royal St. Charles Street and like that in those shoeshine things. And I made nice money. I had about $40 then. And I gave him money to buy me a bow and strings and paid him for the bass. So I never forget. He bought everything and strung the bass up.
And only $7 for the bass?

Yeah, for the bass. Yeah. And I paid him for the rest of the stuff. He bought me strings and the bow and the rosin, everything I had to go with it. And he strung it up for me. He says, well, now right from here you're going to start your scales. And he got one of those bass methods. They have a keyboard on a fingerboard. Yeah. Yeah. So the piano has a keyboard, see. And so he cut that out as a piece of paper and pasted it on my fingerboard. Yeah. Yeah. And from there, we went from there. I started studying that thing. Yeah. Yeah. And he showed me the different keys. Like you see guys when you say, you really, that's, when you study that, those are the notes you're supposed to make the changes.
When you started, were you bowing mostly or picking?

Well, mostly bowing. Because he wanted me to start to, see, that's, that's the, you get the sound on the bass better, like that, see, when you're bowing. So, so I, I did pretty good during the Lent months and, and when the season did open up that Easter, first job I had was with my brother, Isaiah. Oh, yeah. He brought me up with his little band. Just, just that, that one job, you know. I, I played with him. He had a little gig, we call them nowadays. So, one of those picnics. Oh, yeah. On the, on the, on the, Millenburg, yeah. And I went with him. So, gee, I did pretty good. I used to go to rehearsals, you know, with different little groups and carol, just to get in practice like that, you know. But I couldn't play with the, the fast bands. And, but I find myself in the first tune I remember playing was the Sheik of Arab Eve. The first tune.
The time you got on the boat where you, most of the people picked you up at the time?

Oh, well, well, when I was on the boat, I was, was moving pretty nicely, see. But then, I didn't know, I didn't know how to read very fast then, see. And, and fate used to take me and the bass player was with him. See, he had bass player with him. I was the second bass player. He had Bobby Foster on the boat. Well, well, not, not, not then, when, when I was there. The fellow was by the name of Cecil, Cecil Scott, his name was, or the St. Louis. Yeah. No, he was the one. He played, he played bass, he played flute, he played everything. He was just a fanatic of, of instruments, you know. Well, he was playing tuba then, see. And I just played bass, string bass. And I'll never forget it, he was playing four-valve, big bass, tuba. And he used to sit there and fate marveled, and we had two pianos. Love him good. And fate marveled himself, right, right then. They set me between the bass and those two pianos. And in the morning, he'd get up, I'd get up for breakfast on that boat. And, and after breakfast, just him and I, the piano, would go downstairs. And sit on the bandstand. That's why he, he really put, I, I'll never forget that man. He's dead and gone. But then, I've always admired him for that and thanked him.
He helped you.

Because he really, he really did. He helped me. He drilled me from, from the time, from seven o'clock in the morning up until noon, it's time to eat. Then, then the big band rehearsals, see. But, what he used to do, he marked, marked my music, and where, marked the fingering on my instrument. Then I knew a little bass horn, I could play it on either instrument then, see. I got so, coming up, the bass horn, and, and the bass string bass. Because I, I knew, I, I, there's one good thing about it. I started learning the instrument. To know the, the, the finger of the instrument, see. Then, and he just put the fingering under the music. He said, now these same notes, it's just like that. I said, you're supposed to play. And we started, he played the bass on the piano and everything, and like that, and, and up I went. And I stayed with him four years. Four years. And he says, when you, when I turn you loose, you can go. He said, but don't leave until I tell you, you can go. He said, they all leave me. That's what he, he always said. He says, everyone I've had, sooner or later they, they'll leave. And that's what's true. So, so finally I, I, I start getting wires from, uh, Red Allen, New York. You see, I was in St. Louis, you see. So, so, so I went, first year, that last year, I said, I said, well, maybe I might, I might go to New York. So, finally, I was with me, just before, I left, I left the boat, I left the boat, uh, I went to Oklahoma City. Yeah, I left the boat one year. And I went to Oklahoma City with Alvin Fats Wall. I didn't go down New Orleans, you see. And the following summer, we went back on the boat, see. Uh, a boy by the name of Eugene Hill, Slim they call him. He's out in Minnesota now. That's, he's around Chicago now. I, I saw him not very long ago. What did he play? A drummer. He was a drummer, yes. And, uh, God gifted music world. That's what you see, you know, I am Eugene Hill, God gifted music world. So, so, so, so him and I, we went out in Oklahoma City, a fellow by the name of Alvin Fats Wall, a fine musician. And that's where I ran into another fast, fast group. All fine musicians. Young and new. They, they can read. But I was ready, though. I was ready for them. And I think that helped me a hundred percent, because when I left there and come back on the boat, I was really walking. And I would sit right in there with feet and him. And he was just laughing. He says, oh yeah, you're getting slick now, eh. You know, that's what he used to tell me. Well, I said, so, I made one, one season with them in St. Louis. And so, I, I, I told him, I says, I says, I think, I said, I got a wire from Ray Allen. I said, I think I'm going, I'm going to New York. He says, well, well, Al, he says, I must tell you. He said, well, you ready? He said, you just go ahead on. If you want to go, it's okay. I won't stop you, but I want you to go when you was right. I said, you ready? You tell him I sent you. Just like that. That's the way he used to talk. You tell him I sent you. So, when I left there, I had my bass horn and bass fiddle, and I could play both of them. And as years rolled by, I got to New York, and start getting around with fast company, and everybody, I must be ready, because everybody was somebody I'd sit in and played with, with the best around New York.
I remember those records you made with, um, Red Allen.

Yeah, oh, Billy Banks, all the Dixieland group. I made a lot of recordings with them, and I played with some of the best bands in different combinations. Tommy Dossie, Mount, Mount City Blue Blows, Tommy Dossie, all those guys, Coleman Hawkins.
I'm trying to think, did you belong to any big band during the 30s? Yes, Cab Calloway.
That's what I was trying to think of. Yeah, Cab Calloway. That was my first big band.
Who's the other bass player? Is Rhythm in New York now? Oh, Hinton. Milton Hinton, yeah.
Milton Hinton, yeah.
I was confused. I knew he was Rhythm. I couldn't remember.

Hinton, uh, no, yeah. After I left, Hinton took my place, because I was right here in California. See, I stayed out in California around 34. I didn't go back with Cab. I come out here with Cab a long time before. Then, then I went back east in 40, a little before the war, see. Yeah. And I went back with Les Hyde Band from here, from the west coast, the great Les Hyde. We went to the, uh, the Golden Gate. That's when the Golden Gate was in New York, a big place. Yeah, remember that. I stayed with Les for a short while. When I got back to New York, everybody wanted me to stay there, so I decided I would just stay there. I would just stay in New York. That's where Jimmy Ryan come in, see. Now we, now we're on the right road.
That's where I'm going.

So, when I first went in, Jimmy Ryan, Jimmy Ryan wasn't anything about, uh, it just was a little, little place. Yeah. Wasn't known at all. We, we made it popular then. It was Zutty Singleton. Oh, yeah. I was with Zutty Singleton. Oh, yeah. And Joe Elridge, uh, Roy Elridge, uh, brother. That's right. Yeah. Yeah. And Don Fry, Don Fry, Don Fry pianist. Yeah, I remember. He's still there, I heard. She's been there for many years.
I first heard him at Missouri down at the Vanguard.
Yeah, Village Vanguard, yeah. That's, that's where I first heard him. At Village Vanguard.
Then when did you go to Boston?

Well, then, right, right after I closed at Jimmy Ryan's, and, uh, then it was during the war then. So this fellow, Sabie Lewis, from Boston, had a very fine little eight piece swinging band. They were all fine musicians. They played a lot of modern and good swing music, see. So, I met him, it was my closing week. We was one block apart. He was at Kelly's stable, and, and I was down to Ryan, see. So, I passed by there, I heard a little band swinging, so I walked in. Kelly said, we were always dropping different clubs when you were around the streets, see. So, I slept a long time. So the guys, they were all looking at me, and that. So, then when they come down up the stands, and I introduced myself to them. So, Sabie says, oh, yeah. So the guy says, gee, you, the Vanguard used to play at Cav. Oh, and we, and so on. So, he says, well, what are you doing now? I says, I'm just, I'm closing down here. This week. He says, you are? He says, well, listen, this is my bass player. He's got to go back to Boston to go to the Navy. They, they drafted me in the Army, see. The Navy. So, he says, would you, would you like to take the job or come sit in with you, stay with us? We have two more weeks here before we leave, see. I says, well, I says, I said, well, maybe I would. He says, I'll let you know. He says, well, we're having a rehearsal tomorrow. Would you come down and rehearse with us? I says, yes, gladly. And he says, no. He says, stay in there, play a set with us. I said, well, all right. And I sat in with them and played a set, and man, and so they had a lot of music. They had plenty of music. That's all they did was reading, you know, heavy arrangements. For a small group, they played, they sounded like a big band, a big band sound, see. Because they had, they had two trumpets, three saxophones, and three rhythms, see. And baritone, tenor, and alto. That's how these, oh boy, these are really junk. So, so I sat in and played with them. So, and I said, that's wonderful. He says, will you come and make rehearsals with us tomorrow? I says, okay, I'll sit in. Then I started rehearsing with the guys, and so that, that week before the boy, when he left, and I closed down there, and I opened up with him. And I stayed there, I tell you, stay for two weeks, and found when they got ready to go back to Boston, so he asked me to go to Boston. That was the problem then, see. I says, well, I don't want to leave New York. He says, well, would you just, just go to Boston and open up with us, since you play with the band, you'll, you'll, you'll understand it and everything, so just open up with us, stay a week if you don't like it, or you don't have to stay, you know, until we can get somebody, you know, like that, around Boston. I says, well, I says, okay. I said, because going back, and going to Boston, that means I have to, I have to do a lot of things. I brought up a lot of things. I had a nice little apartment and everything, you know. So I had to tear down, and pack up, and go with, with things. So, so when I got there, I went there for one week to stay, and I stayed 18 years. How long? Yeah, 18 years. How did you come out here now? Yeah, well, I come, I come back about a year ago. Yeah. See, when I went back to Boston, and doing, and a little after the war, and after all the boys, and everybody started on this modern jazz and kick, so some of the boys, and feel though that they wasn't, a little bit up on everything that happened, so they, Boston is the greatest field for music, you know, schools, you got all those conservatories. I know Boston, somebody, huh? So, so gee, and I look back and stuff, I say, well, I've been playing a long time, and I said, and I know practically every type of music there is, and coming up during my time, I play. Please.

I played the mix of land, I played swing, and here's this modern jazz coming, says everybody's going to study. I says, well, I'm going to join the rest of them. He says, nothing to do. I didn't do anything in the daytime, so I went on studying. I wound up three and a half years in New England Conservatory, see? And that's why I had very good training. So then we played, I played, it was progressive music. As a matter of fact, I like all music, all types of music. It's all good when it's played good. That's right. Most people will ask you, what do you like? You like this jazz better? They're like, it's all good when it's played good. That's right. Because Dixieland, they have good Dixieland, they have bad Dixieland. I've heard some Dixieland bands, it's terrible. I know some guy probably will eat my head off, but it's true. Never overestimate. No, no, it's true. I've heard some bad swing. I've heard some bad progressive jazz. And it's rock and roll, everything. I like it all, as long as it's good. Because that soul of music, regardless what type of music there is, I played lots of semi-classics in the school symphonies, you know. See what's going. And it's just good music. Once you're a musician, you get that in your soul, and your love, love of music. You've got to learn to love any type, and know it.
I was going to ask you to make a little message to your brothers, if you'd like to. I mean, I'm not... We forgot to mention the Esquire. You might mention that.

Yes. Yes, Esquire. That was in the... I was still with Sabah Lewis' band, see, up in Boston. I didn't know anything about it, told several fans. One night I was up in Portland, Maine, playing a Saturday night dance out on the... the Old Archie, Old Archie Beach. So they asked me, says, gee, I heard you made Esquire. I says, I don't know. He says, sure. And one of the fans had the poll, you know. So, gee, I says, well, I'm glad somebody thought of me. He says, you... Yes, boy. She says, I know everybody. They voted for you. He says, well, that's great. Then, well, then I went from there. We had a job in New York at the Zanzibar. That's where we enlarged the band. We had about 16, 17 piece band because we played the big Zanzibar show, see. And they present the trophy to me there. That's 1944. I was made for Esquire, All-American. The bass player.
That's a great big award. We might take a picture of it so we can see it.
Yes. Your brother would be glad to see it.
Thanks for having me, too. Do you want to say hello to your brother?

Yes, I'll say hello to Isaiah and Andrew. And I wish them the very best of health. And I'm all right myself. And doing pretty good, as a musician do, you know. And I hope everything turned out right. I was very sorry to hear about my brother Robert Pass. Of course, we all have to go that way sometimes, you see. So, later on I might make a trip to New Orleans. I'm planning on making a trip very shortly. Either driving or come there with a little combination. Joe Dansberg. You know Joe Dansberg?
I haven't seen him. Yeah.
He made the Yellow Dog Blues. Yeah, well everybody knows that all over the country.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. It's a jukebox hit down in New Orleans.
Yes. Well, I made that recording with him.
I didn't even know you were out here until I saw your name on that record.
Oh, yeah. Then I knew where you were. Yeah. I thought you were still in Boston maybe. They're a very nice little group.
Yeah, it was a good band.
Well. So, it was nice meeting you and I think we had a nice interview. Yes, I certainly enjoyed it. Thanks a lot.
Thank you very much.
I hope we meet again soon.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: Opening, name and birth date
segments.summary: Morgan gives his name and says he was born August 19, about 1912, on the day of the interview.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: Brother Sam's band and the Marrero bass players
segments.summary: Morgan recalls his oldest brother Sam playing trumpet and his early love of bass, especially Simon Marrero. He and Allen discuss the Marrero brothers and their father Billy.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: Growing up near the French Market; the Morgan brothers
segments.summary: He was raised around Ursuline and Dauphin. His Baptist family had no musicians until Sam began, followed by his other brothers.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: Parades, funerals and second liners
segments.summary: He remembers watching parades and funeral bands as a boy, and gang fights among the second liners.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: First instrument bass; Yank Johnson and Alfred Williams in Sam's band
segments.summary: Bass was his first instrument. He remembers trombonist Yank Johnson and drummer Alfred Williams in Sam's band.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in New Orleans
segments.title: Sam's and Isaiah's bands: banjo players and the two Morgan bands
segments.summary: Morgan and Allen try to recall the banjo player and bassists in Sam's band. He explains there were two Morgan bands, including Isaiah's with Jim Little.

segments.title: Other New Orleans bass players he admired
segments.summary: He recalls a small bassist with a big bass in Sam's band, and old man Kimball, and trades names such as Jimmy Brown and Manuel Perez.

segments.title: Simon Marrero teaches him to bow and repair bass
segments.summary: Simon Marrero taught him to read and bow, and he practically lived at Marrero's house. He started in his teens.

segments.title: Johnny Lindsay, Piron's bassist, and learning tuba with David Jones
segments.summary: They discuss Johnny Lindsay and the Cuban bassist with Piron. Morgan says David Jones gave him his first tuba lessons at the Astoria Roof.

segments.title: Bass method and studying the hard way
segments.summary: He describes starting on a four-string bass and studying with Marrero's method book, with little other teaching.

segments.title: The Astoria Roof job and Fate Marable's offer
segments.summary: At the Astoria Roof he played in David Jones's band until Fate Marable heard him and invited him onto the boat, despite his not reading music.

segments.title: Buying his first bass and first job with Isaiah
segments.summary: He bought a bass for $7 from Marrero with shoeshine money. Marrero pasted a paper keyboard on the fingerboard. His first job was a picnic gig with Isaiah.

segments.title: Second bassist on Marable's boat
segments.summary: On Marable's boat he was second bass player behind Cecil Scott, seated between the bass and two pianos. Marable coached him.

segments.title: Four years with Marable, Oklahoma City, and leaving for New York
segments.summary: Marable drilled him daily and marked his music. He left for a year in Oklahoma City, returned, then left for New York on Red Allen's wire with Marable's blessing.

segments.chapter: New York and the swing years
segments.title: Recordings in New York with Red Allen and others
segments.summary: In New York he recorded with Red Allen, Billy Banks, the Mound City Blue Blowers and Coleman Hawkins.

segments.chapter: New York and the swing years
segments.title: Cab Calloway, California, and the Les Hite band
segments.summary: Calloway's was his first big band; Milton Hinton replaced him. He stayed in California around 1934, then returned east in 1940 with Les Hite.

segments.chapter: New York and the swing years
segments.title: Jimmy Ryan's with Zutty Singleton and Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: He joined Jimmy Ryan's when it was a little unknown place. Players included Zutty Singleton, Roy Eldridge's brother and a pianist.

segments.title: Joining Sabby Lewis and moving to Boston
segments.summary: He met Sabby Lewis's band at Kelly's Stable, replaced the bassist leaving for the Navy, and went to Boston for what became 18 years.

segments.title: New England Conservatory and liking all kinds of music
segments.summary: In Boston he studied at the New England Conservatory for three and a half years. He says all music is good when played well.

segments.title: Winning the Esquire award in 1944
segments.summary: With Sabby Lewis he learned in Portland, Maine, that he had won the Esquire poll and received the trophy at the Zanzibar in New York.

segments.title: Hello to his brothers
segments.summary: Morgan sends greetings to Isaiah and Andrew and regrets his brother Robert's death. He plans a trip to New Orleans.

segments.title: Joe Darensbourg and the Yellow Dog Blues recording
segments.summary: Morgan mentions Darensbourg's Yellow Dog Blues hit, on which he played. Allen saw his name on the record.

segments.title: Goodbyes
segments.summary: They thank each other and end the interview.
